Displacement reckoning surface. Triggered when cumulative inbound displacement to RBiH-controlled municipalities crosses 100,000 persons. The historical reference set: the Research and Documentation Centre Sarajevo (RDC) Bosnian Book of Dead and the UNHCR figures cited at Prosecutor v. Stakić IT-97-24-T paras. 700-716). This annotation registers the reception-side strain — supply degradation and cohesion erosion in absorbing municipalities — as the documentary counterpart to the displacement record. Civilian-protection legal standard: Geneva Convention IV Article 49.

When the displaced-in origin OSID set intersects an enclave municipality, the joint observation (origin: enclave; destination: RBiH-government area) is recorded for Dayton-scoring narrative. The ledger does not flip rupture wiring or enclave_resilience aggregates; it ensures the endgame reckoning can describe the demographic flow truthfully — which enclaves emptied where, on which trajectory, and across which turn window. Tribunal-observation reckoning surface. Triggered when cumulative war_crimes_events exceeds 3 with international_standing below 45. The historical referent is the establishment of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia by UN Security Council Resolution 827 (25 May 1993) under Chapter VII authority, with subject-matter jurisdiction defined by Articles 2 (grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions), 3 (violations of the laws or customs of war), 4 (genocide), and 5 (crimes against humanity) of the ICTY Statute. The Tribunal operated from The Hague between 1993 and 2017 and indicted 161 persons across all parties to the conflict. Audit-only framing applies: this annotation registers a documentary observation in the endgame Cost Ledger; it does not flip rupture wiring, does not unlock atrocity-tactic paths, and does not attribute culpability to any specific individual or unit. The legal standard for any specific finding is the Tribunal's own jurisprudence (Tadić IT-94-1, Galić IT-98-29-T, Krstić IT-98-33, Mladić IT-09-92, Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T, Prlić IT-04-74-T, Dragomir Milošević IT-98-29/1).

Counterfactual reckoning surface. UN Security Council Resolution 824 (6 May 1993) and Resolution 836 (4 June 1993) designated Sarajevo, Tuzla, Žepa, Goražde, Bihać and Srebrenica as Safe Areas under UNPROFOR mandate. The historical record finds the Safe Area regime structurally failed: ICTY Trial Chamber, Prosecutor v. Krstić (IT-98-33-T, 2 August 2001, paras. 36-46) documents the July 1995 collapse of the Srebrenica enclave and the genocide that followed, and Prosecutor v. Mladić (IT-09-92-T, 22 November 2017, paras. 2493-2581) finds command responsibility for that collapse. This annotation records a sustained run-state in which the Safe Area mandate is enforced past t145 — the counterfactual that the international protection framework on paper had been honoured in practice. The annotation describes the documented institutional regime; it does not attribute culpability for any specific historical event.

Triggered after prior third_party_arms_channel firing under patron_pressure above 35: the documented late-cycle international-mediator pressure that compresses an alternate supply route already operating under formal embargo. The historical referent is the so-called Croatia Pipeline / Iran Channel documented at Wiebes, *Intelligence and the War in Bosnia 1992-1995* (NIOD, 2002), ch. 4-5, and the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Report on the Bosnian Arms Pipeline (8 November 1996), describing the April 1994 — 1995 transhipment through Croatia under tacit U.S. acquiescence and the parallel UNSC Resolution 713 (25 September 1991) arms-embargo regime. Equipment quality minus 4 percent for 20 turns reflects mediator-pressure attenuation of the alternate pipeline as the 1995 international consensus on the arms-control posture shifted toward the Dayton lift-and-balance framework. Audit-only annotation; the embargo lawfulness question and the Croatia-side facilitation question are both subject to documentary record outside the engine surface.
